parsed.hook: Sonnenuhr slate tilts so steeply that vineyard workers tie themselves to posts; that 70-degree slope is why this Auslese keeps 70 g/L sugar yet finishes at 7% alcohol. The 2020 carries 9.5 g acidity that tastes like lime cordz under slate dust.
parsed.wine_summary: Fritz Haag’s holdings sit dead-center on the Mosel’s Middle Terrace, a 200-million-year-old Devonian slate reef that here faces full south above the river bend. The family has bottled site-specific Rieslings since 1925; today Wilhelm Haag ferments only with ambient yeasts, stops the cool tank fermentations early, then leaves the wine on fine lees until Easter so the residual sugar integrates without tasting cloying. In 2020 the Juffer-Sonnenuhr parcel (0 0.8 ha of un-grafted 70-year-old vines rooted in blue slate) gave 65 hl/ha, half the legal maximum, concentrating the aromatics to the point where the wine carries 95 g/L residual sugar yet feels weightless.
parsed.terroir_expression: Devonian grey-blue slate weathers into thin, plate-like sheets that reflect heat back onto the berries at night; the rock’s high mica content stores daytime warmth and releases it slowly, lengthening ripening into late October. Because the slate is so brittle, roots dive 8–10 m through fissures to find water, picking up potassium that buffers natural acidity and flinty minerals that translate into a struck-match note on the finish. The river’s 180° loop just below the site funnels cool air up-slope at dusk, locking in riesling’s citrus oils and preventing botrytis until the very last pick.
parsed.vinification_summary: Whole-cluster pressing at 0.9 bar preserves aromatics, then 75% ferments in 1,000 L stainless steel at 14 °C; the remainder sees 60-year-old 1,200 L Mosel fuder for six weeks to add palate grip through micro-oxidation. Fermentation arrests at 7–8% ABV by chilling to 4 °C, leaving 65–95 g/L RS that is balanced by 8.5–9.5 g TA (tartaric equivalent) — a ratio that keeps the wine technically medium-sweet yet sensorially off-dry.
parsed.food_pairing: Nashville hot chicken sandwich — the sugar douses cayenne while the acid slices through fry oil. Thai green papaya salad with dried shrimp — lime and chili echo the wine’s citrus and residual sweetness. Fine-dining: seared scallop with cauliflower purée and yuzu kosho — briny shellfish, nutty purée and fragrant citrus all mirror the wine’s layered profile.
parsed.comparable_wines: Dr. Loosen Ürziger Würzgarten Auslese — red slate gives spicier aromatics but similar sugar-to-acid tightrope. Willi Schaefer Graacher Domprobst Auslese — more slate-driven smoke, slightly lighter frame. Egon Müller Scharzhofberger Auslese — greater botrytis, more apricot, twice the price.
parsed.style_profile: High-acid medium-sweet Riesling with slate-driven smoke and lime-oil lift
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink 2026-2045; keep at 10°C and 70% RH — the sugar and acid will polymerize into petrol and honey notes after 12–15 years.
parsed.value_assessment: US $45-55 per 375 mL; same bracket as Selbach-Oster BA but Fritz Haag gives you true Auslese concentration for Spätlese money. Worth it if you like Mosel tension without botrytis weight.
parsed.market_position: Lists in two-Michelin-star German restaurants and niche Manhattan retailers; casual riesling drinkers rarely see it because quantities are under 1,500 cases total.
parsed.insider_take: Ignore the medals on the neck — judging panels reward sugar without checking balance. The real tell is the 9 g acidity that keeps the 95 g sugar airborne; if you think all auslesen are syrupy this bottle will reset your compass.
